result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Clustered Data: ICC and the Design Effect" subtitle: "Why observations are not independent · intra-class correlation · design effect · effective sample size · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Regression workshop: every row was an **independent** person - Today: people live in **villages**, wards, clinics or schools, and are measured **repeatedly** - By the end you can: - spot **clustered** and **repeated** data - compute and explain the **ICC** - compute the **design effect** and the **effective sample size** - say why a **naive** analysis gives standard errors that are too small ::: ## Our data: a village blood-pressure trial ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **40 villages**, randomised 20 + 20 to a **hypertension programme** or usual care (synthetic data) - **20 adults per village**, so **800 people** - SBP measured at **0, 3, 6 and 12 months** (some visits missing) - The **programme is given to a whole village**: the unit of randomisation is the village ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bp |> select(village, arm, person, age, months, sbp) |> head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 6 village arm person age months sbp 1 V01 Programme V01-P01 64 0 135 2 V01 Programme V01-P01 64 3 149 3 V01 Programme V01-P01 64 6 134 4 V01 Programme V01-P01 64 12 131 5 V01 Programme V01-P02 38 0 121 6 V01 Programme V01-P02 38 3 136 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Levels and clusters {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Levels in the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bp |> summarise(villages = n_distinct(village), people = n_distinct(person), rows = n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 villages people rows 1 40 800 2782 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} **Visit** (level 1) inside **person** (level 2) inside **village** (level 3). Rows that share a person or a village are **more alike** than rows that do not: they are **correlated**. ::: ::: {.incremental} - **Clustered** data: people grouped in villages (one measurement each) - **Repeated** (longitudinal) data: the same person measured several times - Here we have **both** ::: ## Why this matters ::: {.warn} Most methods you know (linear and logistic regression, t-test, chi-square) assume **independent** observations. With correlated observations the **estimates** are often fine, but the **standard errors, CIs and p-values are wrong**, usually **too small**. ::: ::: {.incremental} - Ten people from one village are not ten independent pieces of information - The **effective** sample size is smaller than the number of rows - The problem is largest for a **cluster-level** exposure, such as our programme ::: # Topic 2 — The ICC {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Villages differ ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} b0 <- bp |> filter(months == 0) b0 |> group_by(village, arm) |> summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(mean_sbp) |> mutate(village = fct_inorder(village)) |> ggplot(aes(mean_sbp, village, colour = arm)) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_vline(xintercept = mean(b0$sbp), linetype = 2) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_blue, col_red)) + labs(x = "Mean baseline SBP (mmHg)", y = "Village", colour = NULL) + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_clustered_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} At **baseline**, before any programme, village means range from about **120 to 141 mmHg**. With 20 random people per village we would expect much less spread. ::: ## The intra-class correlation ::: {.eq} ICC = σ²~between villages~ / (σ²~between villages~ + σ²~within villages~) ::: ::: {.incremental} - The **share of the total variance** that lies **between** clusters - Also the **correlation** between two people from the same village - **0**: clusters do not matter. **1**: everyone in a cluster is identical - In community health ICCs are often small (**0.01 to 0.1**), but they still matter when clusters are large ::: ## Estimating the ICC ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m0 <- lmer(sbp ~ 1 + (1 | village), data = b0) VarCorr(m0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Groups Name Std.Dev. village (Intercept) 4.317 Residual 15.299 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} icc(m0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # Intraclass Correlation Coefficient Adjusted ICC: 0.074 Unadjusted ICC: 0.074 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} ICC **= 0.074**: about **7%** of the variation in baseline SBP is **between villages**. It looks small. The next slide shows why it is not. ::: # Topic 3 — The design effect {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Design effect and effective sample size ::: {.eq} DEFF = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC n~eff~ = n / DEFF ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} deff <- 1 + (20 - 1) * 0.074 c(design_effect = deff, effective_n = 800 / deff) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` design_effect effective_n 2.4060 332.5021 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - m = **cluster size** (20 per village) - DEFF **2.4**: the variance is 2.4 times what a simple random sample would give - The 800 people carry the information of only about **330 independent** people - A **small ICC** with **large clusters** still gives a **large** design effect ::: ## The naive analysis at 12 months ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_naive <- lm(sbp ~ arm, data = bp12) summary(fit_naive)$coefficients["armProgramme", ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) -4.0147535818 1.1750745643 -3.4165947455 0.0006733127 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} The estimate (about **−4.0 mmHg**) is fine, but its **SE (1.2)** treats 657 people as independent. The honest SE is about **1.4 times larger**. ::: ## One valid simple analysis ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vm12 <- bp12 |> group_by(village, arm) |> summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp), .groups = "drop") t.test(mean_sbp ~ arm, data = vm12) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: mean_sbp by arm t = 2.6681, df = 37.93, p-value = 0.01116 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Control and group Programme is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 1.032151 7.525524 sample estimates: mean in group Control mean in group Programme 128.5770 124.2981 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Reduce each village to **one mean**: 40 independent numbers - The **difference is about 4.3 mmHg** with a CI of **1.0 to 7.5**: the programme works, with an honest p-value - Limits: covariate adjustment is harder, and villages of unequal size are weighted equally - The next sessions give **model-based** alternatives ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `clustered-workshop/labs/lab1_clusters.R` - count villages, people and rows - village means, the **ICC** and the **design effect** - the naive analysis vs the village-level t-test ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tzq4uo.w0fma5" data-show="QWR1bHRzIGluIGEgdmlsbGFnZSB0ZW5kIHRvIHJlc2VtYmxlIGVhY2ggb3RoZXIgbW9yZSB0 aGFuIGFkdWx0cyBlbHNld2hlcmU=" data-explain="UGVvcGxlIGluIHRoZSBzYW1lIHZpbGxhZ2Ugc2hhcmUgZW52aXJvbm1lbnQsIGRpZXQgYW5k IHNlcnZpY2VzLCBzbyB0aGVpciBvdXRjb21lcyBhcmUgY29ycmVsYXRlZC4gVGhpcyBpcyB0 aGUgcmVhc29uIGZvciB0cmVhdGluZyB0aGUgdmlsbGFnZSBhcyBhIGNsdXN0ZXIu"} In this trial the programme is given to whole villages. Which statement about the 800 adults is correct? - Adults in the same village are independent, because each was measured on their own - The village is just a label for location and has no bearing on how the adults are analysed - Adults in a village tend to resemble each other more than adults elsewhere - Villages with many adults should be dropped so that all villages carry equal weight ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tzqi3e.w0g0rj" data-show="QWJvdXQgNyUgb2YgdGhlIHZhcmlhdGlvbiBpbiBTQlAgbGllcyBiZXR3ZWVuIHZpbGxhZ2Vz " data-explain="VGhlIElDQyBpcyB0aGUgc2hhcmUgb2YgdG90YWwgdmFyaWFuY2UgdGhhdCBpcyBiZXR3ZWVu IGNsdXN0ZXJzLiBJdCBpcyBhbHNvIHRoZSBjb3JyZWxhdGlvbiBiZXR3ZWVuIHR3byBwZW9w bGUgZnJvbSB0aGUgc2FtZSBjbHVzdGVyLg=="} A mixed model of baseline SBP gives an ICC of 0.07. What does it say? - Seven percent of the adults in the villages have a raised blood pressure - Two villages differ in their mean SBP by about 7 mmHg on average - The programme is expected to lower SBP by 7% in each treated village - About 7% of the variation in SBP lies between villages ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tzqvc0.w0gf8t" data-show="VGhlIGRlc2lnbiBlZmZlY3QgZ3Jvd3Mgd2l0aCBjbHVzdGVyIHNpemU6IHdpdGggMjAgcGVy IHZpbGxhZ2UgaXQgaXMgbW9yZSB0aGFuIDI=" data-explain="REVGRiA9IDEgKyAobSAtIDEpIHggSUNDLiBXaXRoIG0gPSAyMCBhbmQgSUNDID0gMC4wNyB0 aGUgdmFyaWFuY2UgaXMgbW9yZSB0aGFuIGRvdWJsZWQsIHNvIHRoZSBlZmZlY3RpdmUgc2Ft cGxlIHNpemUgaXMgbGVzcyB0aGFuIGhhbGYgdGhlIG51bWJlciBvZiBwZW9wbGUu"} Why can an ICC of only 0.07 still matter a great deal? - The design effect grows with cluster size: with 20 per village it is more than 2 - A small ICC means the villages are nearly identical, so the programme effect gets hidden - Statistical software rounds a small ICC up to 1 when it computes the standard errors - The ICC becomes relevant just when the study has fewer than about ten villages ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tzr8kq.w0gtq7" data-show="MzMwIHBlb3BsZQ==" data-explain="VGhlIGVmZmVjdGl2ZSBzYW1wbGUgc2l6ZSBpcyBuIGRpdmlkZWQgYnkgdGhlIGRlc2lnbiBl ZmZlY3Q6IDgwMCAvIDIuNCBpcyBhYm91dCAzMzAuIFRoZSBkYXRhIGNhcnJ5IHRoZSBpbmZv cm1hdGlvbiBvZiBhYm91dCAzMzAgaW5kZXBlbmRlbnQgcGVvcGxlLg=="} A design effect of 2.4 with 800 people gives an effective sample size of about... - 1,900 people - 330 people - 800 people - 40 people ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="c1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="tzrlth.w0h87m" data-show="QSB0LXRlc3QgY29tcGFyaW5nIHRoZSA0MCB2aWxsYWdlIG1lYW5zIGJldHdlZW4gdGhlIHR3 byBhcm1z" data-explain="VmlsbGFnZSBtZWFucyBhcmUgaW5kZXBlbmRlbnQgYWNyb3NzIHZpbGxhZ2VzLCBzbyBhIHQt dGVzdCBvbiB0aGVtIGdpdmVzIGFuIGhvbmVzdCBTRS4gQW5hbHlzaW5nIHBlb3BsZSBhcyBp bmRlcGVuZGVudCBpZ25vcmVzIHRoZSBjbHVzdGVyaW5nLCB3aGF0ZXZlciBjb3ZhcmlhdGVz IGFyZSBhZGRlZC4="} Which analysis of the cluster-randomised programme effect is valid and simple? - A t-test comparing the 800 individual values between the arms - A chi-square test of the arm against the village number - A linear model that ignores the village but adds age and sex - A t-test comparing the 40 village means between the two arms ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - Data are **clustered** (people in villages) and/or **repeated** (visits in a person) - **ICC** = share of variance between clusters - **DEFF** = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC; **effective n** = n / DEFF - A naive analysis keeps the estimate but gives **SEs that are too small** - Simple valid fix: analyse **cluster means** ::: **Next:** Session 2: cluster-robust standard errors and GEE

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
